questions.q: What does the 'A' in ACID stand for, and what does it guarantee?
options: Atomicity — all statements in a transaction succeed together, or none do
Availability — the database is always reachable
Authentication — users must log in before a transaction runs
Aggregation — transactions always compute a summary value
questions.explain: This is exactly what COMMIT/ROLLBACK implement from Lesson 72.

options: A transaction can only move the database from one valid state to another, never violating enforced rules
Every query returns identical results across sessions
Data is stored in a consistent font format
Transactions always take the same amount of time to run
questions.explain: If a transaction's changes would break a constraint, the whole transaction fails rather than corrupting the data.

options: Concurrent transactions don't see each other's incomplete, in-progress work
Each transaction runs on a separate physical server
Transactions cannot be rolled back once started
Only one user can connect to the database at a time
questions.explain: One transaction's changes stay invisible to others until it commits — covered further in Lesson 75 (Concurrency and Blocking).

options: Once a transaction commits, its changes survive even a server crash or power failure
A transaction can be rolled back at any point, even after commit
Data is compressed to save storage space
Transactions never take longer than a few seconds
questions.explain: COMMIT is a genuine, permanent write — not just an in-memory marker.

questions.q: Why is understanding ACID practically useful, beyond reciting the acronym?
options: It explains why transactions behave the way they do, helping you reason about what can go wrong with concurrent data access
It's required to pass a certification exam and has no other use
It determines which programming language to use
It only matters for NoSQL databases, not SQL Server
questions.explain: Each letter maps to a real, practical guarantee you rely on when writing multi-statement changes.
